pedagogy.summary: Distinguishing flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes is a foundational classification that young children find genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). It is best taught by handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space — rather than by pictures, and by giving the child a physical test ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat') alongside precise vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube). Instruction, not maturation, moves children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality (van Hiele).
bestPractices: Use real solids and flat cut-outs the child can hold and turn, not drawings — the felt three-dimensionality is what teaches the distinction.
Acknowledge the child's observation, then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle, but it is round every way and you can hold it — that is a sphere.'
Offer a child-friendly discriminator: a flat shape lies on the paper (length and width only); a solid takes up space and can be held and turned (length, width and height).
Sort mixed sets into 'flat' and 'solid', including less familiar solids (cone) and non-prototypical exemplars, and go on 'shape hunts' for solids in the room.
Teach the twin pairs explicitly — circle/sphere, square/cube, triangle/pyramid — so the flat and solid names are not confused.
keyRepresentations: Real objects to handle: ball, cube/box, tin, cone beside paper circle, square, triangle
The 'draw it vs hold it' test
commonMisconceptions: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — calls a ball 'a circle', a cube 'a square', a cone 'a triangle' (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023; Nurnberger-Haag).
Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups the round ball with the round circle because both 'look round' (van Hiele visual level).
Confuses a drawing of a solid with the solid itself — treats a cube drawn on paper as 'solid' because of its name.

learn.summary: Young children (ages 5–6) distinguish flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes. This is genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). A central, curriculum-supported approach is handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space in every direction — supported by a dimensional discriminator ('is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card?') and the explicit twin-pair vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube, and loosely triangle/pyramid, since a pyramid has triangle faces). A paper cut-out can itself be picked up and has a slight thickness, so 'can you pick it up?' is not the reliable test; treat the card as a stand-in for an ideal flat shape. Instruction and experience, not age alone, help move children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality.

activities.title: Hold-and-turn sort with real solids and flat cut-outs
feedback: When the child calls a solid by a flat name ('the ball is a circle'), acknowledge then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle — but it is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere.'

If the child groups round things together regardless of flat/solid, prompt the dimensional test: 'Is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and flat like the shape on a card?' Sort by that, not by how round it looks.
Reinforce correct sorts by naming the twin pair: 'Yes — the thin flat one is a circle, the one that is round in every direction is a sphere.'
activities.rationale: Handling real solids beside flat cut-outs lets the child feel three-dimensionality, which is the property being taught; sorting mixed and non-prototypical sets and naming twin pairs targets the specific confusions documented for this age. The test is framed around taking up space in every direction rather than holdability, because a paper cut-out can also be held.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.

At the van Hiele visual level, shapes are judged by their appearance and viewed as a whole, not by distinguishing parts or properties ('it's a square because it looks like one'); deliberate instruction, not maturation alone, is needed to move children to property-based (descriptive) thinking.
Kindergarten geometry requires children to identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, 'flat') or three-dimensional ('solid').
learnerActions: Gather a mixed set the child can handle: a ball, a cube-shaped box, a pyramid, a tin, a cone, beside a paper circle, square and triangle. The paper shapes can also be picked up and have a tiny thickness, so treat each as a stand-in for the ideal flat shape it represents.
Pick up and turn each object over in your hand. Ask: is it round or thick in every direction so it takes up space (solid), or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card (flat)?
Sort the set into two hoops or bins labelled 'flat' and 'solid'.
Include a cone and other less familiar or non-prototypical solids, not only balls and boxes.
Go on a 'shape hunt' around the room to find more solids (a tin, a ball, a box) and say why each takes up space in every direction.
Name the twin pairs aloud as you sort: circle/sphere, square/cube, and triangle/pyramid (a pyramid has triangle faces, though its base may be a square).
activities.intendedInsight: A flat shape has length and width but (ideally) no thickness, and a paper card stands in for it; a solid takes up space in every direction (length, width and height). 'Round like a circle' is not the same as flat — a ball is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere, not a circle. (For the adult: because a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness, 'can you pick it up?' is not the real test — ask whether the shape takes up space in every direction.)

activities.title: Build a solid from flat paper (pop-up)
feedback: If the child keeps the flat name after building, point out that it now takes up space in every direction: 'This stands up and takes up space in every direction now — it is a cube, not just a square.'
Encourage counting faces to ground the solid/flat difference in something the child can touch.
activities.rationale: Constructing the solid from flat paper makes the flat-to-solid transition concrete and lets the child touch and count faces, grounding the solid name in properties the child can feel.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.
learnerActions: Start with a flat paper net (an unfolded pattern of joined flat shapes) and fold/assemble it into a solid (e.g. a pop-up cube or pyramid).
As the solid takes shape, touch and count its faces, edges and corners (vertices).

Compare the finished solid, which now takes up space in every direction, with the flat sheet you started from. Name the solid and the flat shapes of its faces: a cube has square faces, and a pyramid has triangle faces (a square pyramid also has a square base). The unfolded sheet (the net) is several joined shapes, not one square or triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid takes up space in every direction and has faces you can feel and count, whereas the flat paper it came from only lies in a plane — the same name family splits into a flat word and a solid word.

activities.title: Spin-to-compare on screen (scaffold alongside handling)
feedback: If the child still calls the spun ball a circle, pair it with the physical hold: 'The one that vanished edge-on is flat; the one that stays round in every direction is a sphere.'
Note that the on-screen ball is itself a picture on a flat screen — the rotating model stands in for the real object, so pair it with a real hold-and-turn.
activities.rationale: Rotating a model shows depth from every side and a flat shape vanishing edge-on, a useful visual analogue; it is proposed as a scaffold paired with handling, not a replacement, because a flat screen does not provide the physical, tactile handling of a real object.
learnerActions: On screen, spin a circle and a ball. Watch the circle thin to a line and vanish when turned edge-on, while the ball stays round from every side.
Say why: the ideal circle has no thickness, so it disappears edge-on; the ball is round every way and never flattens — it cannot be a circle, it is a sphere.
Immediately repeat with a real paper circle and a real ball in your hand, turning each to feel that the ball is round in every direction while the card is thin.
activities.intendedInsight: An ideal flat shape has no thickness and disappears edge-on; a solid takes up space from every direction. Rotating a model shows this effect, while handling a real object additionally lets the child feel the three-dimensionality directly, so the two are paired. (A real paper circle is a thin card standing in for the zero-thickness ideal.)

constraints: Handling is central here because it lets the child feel that a ball has depth every way while a cut-out is thin. Screen activities (spin-to-compare, drag-to-sort, tap-to-reveal label cards) are offered alongside handling real objects.

A drag-to-sort flat/solid game can give feedback, but every picture on a flat screen is itself flat — this risks reinforcing appearance-based sorting, so on its own it does not elicit physical handling of real objects.
A sort or multiple-choice check can verify or practise the classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or an explanation; use it as a post-check alongside handling real objects.
Conversation alone does not let a child physically handle a shape or see it take up space; use it to prompt the child to justify a sort rather than as the sole medium.
Everyday mislabelling (ball='circle', box='square') is the main obstacle; always acknowledge the child's accurate observation ('yes, round like a circle') before correcting to the solid name.

A paper cut-out is only an approximation of an ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape: it can be picked up and has a slight thickness. So the reliable discriminator is whether the shape takes up space in every direction, not whether it can be physically held — ask the child about the mathematical shape the thin card represents.

Distinguish the drawn solid from the real one: a cube drawn on a page is flat on that page even though its name is 'cube'; contrast the drawing (whose corners you cannot grasp) with a real cube that takes up space in every direction. When naming an example a cube, use a cube-shaped object, since a generic box need not be a cube.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed the 3-D interactive as the 'recommended' artefact while also stating the true lesson is physical handling; this rewrite demotes the screen rotation to an explicit scaffold paired with real objects and foregrounds the hands-on sort and pop-up build, without claiming either medium is the sole means of learning.

Original catalog text included claims that a flat screen 'cannot show' the property and that talk 'cannot convey' dimensionality. These are retained only as narrowly scoped affordances in constraints, not as universal laws; a screen model and conversation can still support learning as scaffolds.

The original row's discriminator ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat' / 'a solid can be held and turned') is an idealisation error: a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness. The guidance now tests whether a shape takes up space in every direction and treats the paper card as an approximation of the ideal flat shape; this correction is applied in the activities and constraints, not only here.

probeDeeper: Can you pick the circle up off the paper and turn it over in your hand? What about the ball?
The ball looks round like a circle — so why do we call it solid and the circle flat?
Here is a cone. Is it flat or solid? How can you tell?
Draw a circle on the paper, then find something in the room that is solid and round like a ball.
assess.correctAnswer: Puts the paper circle and square with the flat shapes and the ball and cube with the solids; explains that the ball is solid because it is round in every direction and you can hold and turn it and it takes up space, whereas the circle just lies flat on the paper — so the ball is a sphere, not a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies a flat (2-D) name to a solid object — shown a real ball or cube, calls it 'a circle' or 'a square' and sorts it with the flat shapes
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hand the child the object to hold and turn: 'a circle is flat on the paper; the ball is round every way and you can pick it up — that is a sphere'; teach the twin-pair names
errorPatterns.distractor: The ball is round, so it is a circle — it goes with the flat shapes
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the solid with a 2-D word and places it in the flat group

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups round things together regardless of whether they are flat or solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the physical test — can you hold it and turn it over, or does it only lie on the paper? — and sort by that, not by look
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts the ball with the circle 'because they both look round'

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses a drawing of a solid with a real solid — judges by the name, so a cube drawn on paper is called 'solid' or a real object 'flat' inconsistently
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast the drawn cube (flat on the page, you cannot grasp its corners) with the real cube you can hold and turn
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls a picture of a cube 'solid' but cannot say the drawing itself is flat on the page

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by the name or overall look — calls the ball a 'circle' and groups it with the flat shapes because it is round.
responseLevels.full: Classifies by dimensionality — flat shapes lie on the paper, solids take up space and can be held and turned — justifies the ball as solid despite looking round, and extends the rule to unfamiliar solids.
responseLevels.partial: Sorts the familiar cases (paper circle flat, ball solid) correctly but by rote naming; cannot say what makes one flat and the other solid, and slips on less familiar solids such as a cone.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a ball, a paper circle, a cube (box) and a paper square. Sort them into 'flat' shapes and 'solid' shapes. Then tell me: why isn't the ball flat, even though it looks round like the circle?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps dimensionality classes the ball as solid despite it 'looking round like a circle'; a child at the naming/visual level calls the ball a 'circle' and puts it with the flat shapes because both look round. The reason tier ('why isn't the ball flat?') separates 'it is round every way and you can hold it' from silence or 'because it is a circle'.
